candidates.extract: Seven Sisters Market is a covered London market in the South Tottenham area of the London Borough of Haringey. The market is owned by Places for London (a wholly owned subsidiary of Transport for London).

candidates.name: Seven Sisters station
candidates.description: London Underground and London Overground station
candidates.extract: Seven Sisters is an interchange station in the Seven Sisters area of the London Borough of Haringey, north London. It is on the Victoria line of the London Underground and the Weaver line of the London Overground.

candidates.name: Marcus Garvey Library
candidates.extract: The Marcus Garvey Library in Tottenham, North London, first opened in 1987. It is a branch of Haringey Libraries run by the London Borough of Haringey and is open seven days a week.

candidates.name: Bruce Grove railway station
candidates.extract: Bruce Grove is a station on the Weaver line of the London Overground, located in central Tottenham in the London Borough of Haringey, north London. It is 6 mi down the line from London Liverpool Street and is situated between and stations.

candidates.name: Brook Street Chapel
candidates.extract: Brook Street Chapel is a church building in Tottenham, North London. The building was constructed for use as a meeting place for local Christians affiliated with the Plymouth Brethren movement.

candidates.name: Tottenham Town Hall
candidates.extract: Tottenham Town Hall is a municipal building in Town Hall Approach Road, Tottenham, London. It is a Grade II listed building.

candidates.name: Tottenham War Services Institute
candidates.extract: The Tottenham War Services Institute (TWSI) was founded by a deed of trust in 1920.

candidates.name: Broadwater Farm
candidates.extract: Broadwater Farm, often referred to simply as "The Farm", is an area in Tottenham, North London, straddling the River Moselle. The eastern half of the area is dominated by the Broadwater Farm Estate ("BWFE"), an experiment in high-density social housing, loosely based on Corbusian ideas, dominated by concrete towers connected by walkways (the controversial, so-called "Streets in the sky"), built in the late 1960s using cheap but fire-vulnerable pre-fabricated concrete panels.
